cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: The form and meaning of each variable in a dataset: numeric values such as age or price, categorical values such as city or product type, ordered categories such as satisfaction level, text, images, audio, dates, and time-series observations. The data type determines how a model can consume the feature.
cards.learningType: Not a learning method; it is a foundation concept used before supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.
cards.taskType: Applies to every task type because classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, forecasting, and generation all require suitable input representation.
cards.highLevel: You inspect each column, decide whether it is continuous, discrete, categorical, ordinal, temporal, or unstructured, then choose transformations such as scaling, one-hot encoding, embeddings, date extraction, image resizing, or text tokenization. Correct typing also affects missing-value handling and validation rules.
cards.whenUse: Use this at the start of every ML project. For example, house price models treat square footage as numeric, neighborhood as categorical, and sale date as temporal; an NLP model treats a review as text rather than a normal categorical column.
cards.limitations: A column can be technically stored as one type but semantically mean another, such as ZIP codes stored as numbers. Incorrect typing leads to wrong preprocessing, meaningless distances, data leakage, and model behavior that looks accurate but fails in production.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A machine-learning setup where every training example includes input features and a known target answer. The target may be a class label such as churn yes/no or a numeric value such as next-month revenue.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Mainly classification and regression; it can also support ranking and structured prediction when labels are available.
cards.highLevel: The algorithm compares its predictions with known labels, calculates an error or loss, and updates model parameters or decision rules to reduce that error. After training, it applies the learned relationship between features and target to unseen examples.
cards.whenUse: Use it when historical labeled data exists and you need predictions: fraud detection from past fraud labels, medical risk scoring from patient outcomes, price prediction from past sales, or email spam classification from labeled emails.
cards.limitations: It depends heavily on label quality and representativeness. Labels may be expensive, biased, outdated, or inconsistent, and the model can learn shortcuts from historical data instead of causal patterns.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A setup where the model receives data without target labels and tries to discover structure, similarity, lower-dimensional representations, unusual observations, or latent groups on its own.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Mostly clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation, association discovery, and anomaly detection.
cards.highLevel: The algorithm optimizes an internal notion of structure rather than matching known labels. Examples include minimizing within-cluster distance, preserving local neighborhoods in a map, estimating probability density, or reconstructing data through a compressed representation.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you do not have labels or you want to explore data: segment customers by behavior, visualize high-dimensional embeddings, detect unusual transactions, or discover topics in a large collection of documents.
cards.limitations: The output is often subjective and difficult to validate. Clusters or components may not correspond to business reality, results can change with scaling and hyperparameters, and interpretation often requires domain expertise.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A learning paradigm where an agent repeatedly chooses actions in an environment and receives rewards or penalties. The goal is to learn a policy that maximizes long-term cumulative reward, not just immediate accuracy.
cards.learningType: Neither supervised nor unsupervised in the usual sense; it is reinforcement learning with rewards, states, actions, and policies.
cards.taskType: Used for sequential decision-making and control rather than standard classification, regression, clustering, or dimensionality reduction.
cards.highLevel: The agent observes a state, chooses an action, receives a reward and a new state, and gradually improves a policy using trial-and-error. It must balance exploration of new actions with exploitation of actions that already seem good.
cards.whenUse: Use it for problems where decisions affect future situations: game playing, robotics, dynamic pricing, ad bidding, traffic signal control, inventory replenishment, and recommendation policies that learn from user interactions over time.
cards.limitations: It can require huge numbers of interactions, carefully designed rewards, and safe simulators. Poor reward design can produce unintended behavior, and policies trained in simulation may fail when transferred to the real world.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A method of dividing labeled data into a training set used to fit the model and a test set held back for an unbiased final performance estimate.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is an evaluation practice used mainly with supervised learning, though similar holdout ideas can be used elsewhere.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification and regression most directly; also useful for forecasting and recommendation evaluation when data is split correctly.
cards.highLevel: You randomly or strategically reserve part of the data before training. The model only learns from the training set, then predictions on the test set are compared with true labels to estimate generalization.
cards.whenUse: Use it for quick model evaluation when you have enough data. For example, train a churn model on 80% of historical customers and test it on the remaining 20% to approximate future performance.
cards.limitations: A random split can be misleading if time order, users, patients, stores, or households overlap across train and test. A single split may also be noisy; with small datasets, cross-validation is usually more stable.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A separate portion of data used during development to compare model choices, tune hyperparameters, choose thresholds, and select features before the final test set is touched.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is an evaluation and model-selection practice.
cards.taskType: Applies mainly to classification and regression, and also to deep learning, forecasting, ranking, and recommendation systems.
cards.highLevel: The model is trained on the training set, evaluated repeatedly on the validation set, and adjusted based on validation performance. The test set remains reserved for one final check after decisions are made.
cards.whenUse: Use it when choosing between models such as logistic regression versus random forest, selecting a learning rate, deciding tree depth, or setting a probability threshold for fraud alerts.
cards.limitations: Repeated decisions based on the same validation set can overfit to it. If the validation set is not representative or leaks information from training, it gives a falsely optimistic picture.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A resampling evaluation method that trains and validates a model multiple times on different splits of the same dataset, then averages the results to estimate performance more reliably.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is an evaluation practice for supervised learning and some unsupervised model-selection workflows.
cards.taskType: Most common for classification and regression; can also support model selection for clustering or dimensionality reduction using suitable metrics.
cards.highLevel: In k-fold cross-validation, data is split into k folds. The model trains on k-1 folds and validates on the remaining fold, repeating until every fold has served as validation. Scores are averaged and variability can be reported.
cards.whenUse: Use it when data is limited or when a single train/validation split is too dependent on luck. It is especially useful for comparing algorithms or tuning hyperparameters in tabular ML.
cards.limitations: It is computationally more expensive because the model is trained multiple times. Standard random folds are invalid for time-series, grouped data, duplicated users, or leakage-prone datasets unless special splitters are used.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: The balance between systematic error from overly simple assumptions, called bias, and sensitivity to random variation in the training data, called variance.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a conceptual framework for diagnosing supervised model behavior.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification and regression, and broadly to any predictive model where generalization matters.
cards.highLevel: High-bias models underfit because they cannot represent the real pattern. High-variance models overfit because they adapt too closely to training noise. Model complexity, regularization, data size, and feature choices shift the balance.
cards.whenUse: Use it when deciding whether to make a model more complex, add regularization, collect more data, simplify features, or diagnose why train and validation scores differ.
cards.limitations: It is a simplification rather than a precise diagnostic in all modern ML settings. Deep learning can show double-descent behavior, and real errors also come from data leakage, label noise, distribution shift, and measurement problems.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A failure mode where a model learns noise, quirks, or accidental patterns in the training data instead of patterns that generalize to new data.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a training/evaluation problem most visible in supervised learning.
cards.taskType: Can affect classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, forecasting, and deep learning whenever a method is too flexible for the available data.
cards.highLevel: The model becomes very accurate on training examples but performs worse on validation or test data. It may memorize rare combinations, react strongly to irrelevant features, or exploit leaked variables.
cards.whenUse: Look for it when training performance is much better than validation performance. Address it with simpler models, regularization, cross-validation, early stopping, dropout, more data, or stricter leakage checks.
cards.limitations: Not every train-test gap is overfitting; distribution shift or label noise can look similar. Also, reducing overfitting too aggressively can cause underfitting and remove useful signal.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A failure mode where a model is too simple, too constrained, poorly trained, or given insufficient features, so it fails to capture important patterns even in the training data.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a training/evaluation problem.
cards.taskType: Can affect classification, regression, clustering, forecasting, and representation learning.
cards.highLevel: The model has high error on both training and validation data. Typical causes include a linear model for a nonlinear problem, too much regularization, too few epochs, poor features, or overly aggressive preprocessing.
cards.whenUse: Diagnose it when both train and validation scores are poor. Fix it by adding informative features, using a more expressive model, reducing regularization, training longer, or improving data quality.
cards.limitations: Increasing complexity can improve training fit but may introduce overfitting. Sometimes poor performance is caused by uninformative labels or missing predictors rather than underfitting alone.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A set of techniques that intentionally constrain a model so it captures stable patterns rather than memorizing noise. Common examples include L1/L2 penalties, dropout, early stopping, tree-depth limits, and data augmentation.
cards.learningType: Not a standalone model; it is a training technique used mostly in supervised and deep learning, with analogs in unsupervised models.
cards.taskType: Applies broadly to classification, regression, representation learning, and generative modeling.
cards.highLevel: Regularization adds a penalty or constraint to the training objective, limits model complexity, injects noise, or stops training before memorization. The goal is lower validation error even if training error becomes slightly higher.
cards.whenUse: Use it when validation performance is worse than training performance, when features are numerous or correlated, or when a flexible model such as a neural network or boosted tree starts to memorize training data.
cards.limitations: Too much regularization causes underfitting. The best amount is data- and model-dependent, so it usually requires validation or cross-validation to tune.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: The process of creating, transforming, selecting, or combining input variables so a model can learn more useful patterns from the raw data.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a data preparation practice used across supervised and unsupervised learning.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, and forecasting.
cards.highLevel: You convert raw information into model-ready signals: extract day-of-week from timestamps, calculate customer tenure, encode categories, aggregate transaction histories, normalize skewed variables, create lag features, or combine domain-specific indicators.
cards.whenUse: Use it when raw columns do not directly express the pattern you need. For example, predicting churn may require features like days since last login, support tickets in 30 days, and change in usage rather than only current account size.
cards.limitations: Manual features can encode bias, leak future information, or become brittle when business processes change. Excessive feature engineering can make pipelines complex and hard to maintain.

cards.heading: A. ML foundations
cards.what: A serious modeling error where information unavailable at prediction time accidentally enters training, validation, or testing, causing performance estimates to be unrealistically high.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a data and evaluation failure mode.
cards.taskType: Can affect classification, regression, clustering, forecasting, recommendation, and any ML system that is evaluated on historical data.
cards.highLevel: Leakage occurs when future outcomes, post-event variables, duplicate records, target-derived features, or preprocessing fitted on the full dataset influence training or evaluation. The model appears strong because it sees clues it would not have in production.
cards.whenUse: Check for it whenever performance seems too good, when data has timestamps, when users or entities repeat, or when features may be created after the target event. Examples include using “refund processed” to predict refund risk or scaling data before splitting.
cards.limitations: Leakage is often subtle and domain-specific. Automated checks rarely catch all cases; preventing it requires understanding when each feature becomes available and designing splits that mimic real deployment.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: A supervised model that predicts a continuous numeric target by fitting a weighted sum of input features, usually assuming an approximately linear relationship between predictors and the outcome.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Regression.
cards.highLevel: It chooses coefficients that minimize prediction error, commonly mean squared error. Each coefficient represents the expected target change for a one-unit feature change, holding other features constant, when assumptions are reasonable.
cards.whenUse: Use it for interpretable numeric prediction and baseline modeling: predicting sales from ad spend, rent from square footage, or delivery time from distance. It is also useful when stakeholders need coefficient-level explanations.
cards.limitations: It struggles with nonlinear relationships, strong interactions, outliers, multicollinearity, and heteroscedastic errors unless features are transformed or regularized. Correlation-based coefficients should not be interpreted as causal without causal design.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: Ridge regression is linear regression with an L2 penalty that discourages large coefficients. It keeps all features but shrinks unstable weights toward zero.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Regression, and conceptually classification when L2 regularization is used in logistic models.
cards.highLevel: It minimizes prediction error plus a penalty proportional to the squared size of coefficients. Correlated or noisy features receive smaller, more stable weights than in ordinary least squares.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you have many numeric features, correlated predictors, or ordinary linear regression coefficients are unstable. It is common in tabular regression, high-dimensional scientific data, and baseline models.
cards.limitations: It does not automatically select features because coefficients usually remain nonzero. It still assumes the engineered feature relationship is roughly linear and requires tuning the regularization strength.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: Lasso regression is linear regression with an L1 penalty that can shrink some coefficients exactly to zero, effectively performing feature selection.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Regression, and conceptually classification when L1 regularization is used in logistic models.
cards.highLevel: It minimizes prediction error plus a penalty proportional to the absolute size of coefficients. Because the L1 penalty has sharp corners, optimization often sets weak or redundant feature coefficients to zero.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you want a sparse, interpretable model from many candidate predictors, such as selecting important marketing variables or biological markers.
cards.limitations: When features are highly correlated, lasso may arbitrarily choose one and discard others. It can underperform ridge when many small effects matter, and the regularization strength must be tuned carefully.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: Elastic net combines L1 and L2 regularization, blending lasso-style feature selection with ridge-style coefficient stabilization.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Regression, with analogous regularized forms for classification.
cards.highLevel: It optimizes prediction error plus both absolute-value and squared-coefficient penalties. The L1 part can zero out weak predictors; the L2 part handles groups of correlated predictors more smoothly.
cards.whenUse: Use it for high-dimensional datasets with correlated features, such as text n-grams, genomics, or many engineered business variables where pure lasso is unstable and pure ridge is not sparse enough.
cards.limitations: It introduces at least two tuning choices: overall penalty strength and L1/L2 mixing ratio. Like other linear models, it needs useful feature transformations for nonlinear patterns.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: A supervised classification model that estimates the probability of a class, most commonly a binary outcome, using a linear combination of features passed through a logistic sigmoid function.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification; it can be extended to multiclass classification through one-vs-rest or multinomial logistic regression.
cards.highLevel: It learns feature weights that maximize the likelihood of the observed labels. The output is a calibrated-ish probability between 0 and 1, and a threshold converts that probability into a class prediction.
cards.whenUse: Use it for interpretable classification baselines such as churn, default risk, disease presence, conversion prediction, or spam detection. It is especially useful when probability estimates and coefficient explanations matter.
cards.limitations: Decision boundaries are linear in the feature space unless you engineer nonlinear features. It can struggle with complex interactions, outliers, class imbalance, and poorly calibrated probabilities if assumptions are violated.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: K-nearest neighbors is an instance-based method that predicts using the labels or values of the most similar training examples, where similarity is usually measured by a distance metric.
cards.learningType: Supervised in its common predictive form; related nearest-neighbor ideas are also used in unsupervised search and retrieval.
cards.taskType: Classification and regression.
cards.highLevel: For a new point, it finds the k closest training points. Classification uses majority vote or distance-weighted vote; regression averages the neighbors’ target values, optionally weighted by distance.
cards.whenUse: Use it for simple baselines, small datasets, recommendation-style similarity tasks, and cases where local similarity is meaningful, such as classifying objects by measurements.
cards.limitations: It becomes slow and memory-heavy on large datasets, is sensitive to feature scaling and irrelevant features, and performs poorly in high-dimensional spaces where distances become less meaningful.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: A family of probabilistic classifiers based on Bayes’ theorem that assumes features are conditionally independent given the class label.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification.
cards.highLevel: It estimates the probability of each class and the likelihood of each feature value under each class. For a new example, it combines these probabilities and chooses the class with the highest posterior probability.
cards.whenUse: Use it for fast text classification, spam detection, sentiment baselines, document topic labeling, and problems with many sparse features such as word counts.
cards.limitations: The independence assumption is often unrealistic, so probability estimates can be poorly calibrated. It may underperform more flexible models when feature interactions are important.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: A tree-shaped supervised model that makes predictions by repeatedly splitting data according to feature-based rules, such as “age < 30” or “income > 50000.”
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification and regression.
cards.highLevel: The algorithm chooses splits that make child nodes more pure for classification or reduce prediction error for regression. A final leaf node stores a class distribution or average target value.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you need transparent rule-based logic, nonlinear relationships, feature interactions, and mixed numeric/categorical data with minimal preprocessing.
cards.limitations: Single trees are unstable and prone to overfitting, especially when grown deep. Small data changes can produce different splits, and greedy split choices may miss globally better structures.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: An ensemble of many decision trees trained on random bootstrap samples and random subsets of features, designed to reduce the instability and overfitting of individual trees.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification and regression.
cards.highLevel: Each tree learns a different view of the data. Predictions are averaged for regression or voted for classification, so individual tree errors tend to cancel out while strong patterns remain.
cards.whenUse: Use it for robust tabular baselines, nonlinear feature interactions, noisy datasets, and situations where you want good performance with limited tuning. It is common in risk scoring, operations, and customer analytics.
cards.limitations: It is less interpretable than a single tree, can be large and slower at prediction, and may not extrapolate beyond the range of training targets. Gradient boosting often outperforms it on structured tabular competitions.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: Support Vector Machine is a supervised method that finds a decision boundary with the largest possible margin between classes; support vector regression adapts the idea to numeric prediction.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Mainly classification; also regression with support vector regression.
cards.highLevel: For classification, it identifies boundary-defining examples called support vectors and maximizes the margin. Kernel functions can implicitly transform data into higher-dimensional spaces for nonlinear boundaries.
cards.whenUse: Use it for medium-sized datasets with clear margins, high-dimensional features, text classification, image-feature classification, or cases where kernelized nonlinear boundaries help.
cards.limitations: It can be slow on large datasets, sensitive to kernel and regularization choices, and less transparent than linear models. Probabilities are not native and often require calibration.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: An ensemble technique that builds many weak models, usually shallow decision trees, sequentially so each new model focuses on correcting errors made by the previous ensemble.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification and regression.
cards.highLevel: The model starts with a simple prediction, calculates residual errors or gradients of a loss function, then adds trees that reduce those errors. Learning rate and tree complexity control how aggressively it improves.
cards.whenUse: Use it for high-performing tabular prediction, ranking, churn, fraud, pricing, and risk models where nonlinear interactions matter and accuracy is more important than simple interpretability.
cards.limitations: It needs careful tuning, can overfit noisy data, and may be harder to interpret and debug. Training can be slower than random forests, although modern implementations are optimized.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: XGBoost is a highly optimized gradient-boosted tree library with regularization, efficient handling of sparse data, shrinkage, column subsampling, and strong performance on structured data.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification, regression, and ranking.
cards.highLevel: It adds decision trees sequentially using gradient and second-order information from the loss function. Regularization, tree pruning, and shrinkage help control overfitting while improving predictive accuracy.
cards.whenUse: Use it for competitive tabular ML, credit scoring, churn, demand prediction, fraud detection, and datasets with many engineered features. It is often a strong default when data is rows-and-columns.
cards.limitations: It has many hyperparameters and can overfit if tuned carelessly. It is less natural for raw images, audio, or long text than deep learning, and explanations usually require tools such as SHAP.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: LightGBM is Microsoft’s gradient-boosted tree framework designed for speed and memory efficiency, especially on large tabular datasets.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification, regression, and ranking.
cards.highLevel: It grows trees leaf-wise rather than level-wise, often reducing loss faster. It also uses histogram-based splitting and techniques such as feature bundling to speed up training.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you need fast training on large structured datasets, many features, or frequent experimentation. It is popular for recommendation features, risk models, and large-scale tabular prediction.
cards.limitations: Leaf-wise growth can overfit small datasets unless depth, number of leaves, and regularization are controlled. Categorical handling and parameter defaults still require validation.

cards.heading: B. Classical supervised algorithms
cards.what: CatBoost is a gradient-boosted tree library especially strong for datasets with categorical variables because it includes built-in categorical encoding strategies.
cards.learningType: Supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification, regression, and ranking.
cards.highLevel: It uses ordered boosting and target-statistic encodings that reduce leakage from categorical variables. Trees are often built symmetrically, which can improve speed and robustness.
cards.whenUse: Use it when your tabular dataset has many categorical fields such as product ID, region, merchant, device type, or user segment, and you want less manual encoding work.
cards.limitations: It can still be computationally heavy, and categorical encodings must be validated carefully for rare categories. Like other boosted models, it is less directly interpretable than linear models or small trees.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: A clustering algorithm that partitions data into k groups by assigning points to the nearest cluster center, called a centroid.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Clustering.
cards.highLevel: You choose k, initialize centroids, assign each point to its nearest centroid, then update centroids to the mean of assigned points. Assignment and update repeat until clusters stabilize.
cards.whenUse: Use it for quick segmentation when clusters are roughly spherical and similar in size: customer behavior segments, image color quantization, grouping stores by metrics, or creating prototype vectors.
cards.limitations: You must choose k in advance. It is sensitive to scaling, outliers, initialization, and non-spherical clusters, and it may force clusters even when the data has no natural grouping.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: A clustering family that builds a tree of nested groups, showing relationships at multiple levels rather than requiring one fixed number of clusters from the start.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Clustering.
cards.highLevel: Agglomerative clustering starts with each point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest clusters according to a linkage rule such as single, complete, average, or Ward linkage. The result is a dendrogram.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you want to explore nested structure, compare cluster granularity, or visualize similarity among samples, documents, genes, products, or customer types.
cards.limitations: It can be slow and memory-intensive for large datasets. Results depend strongly on distance metric and linkage choice, and early merge decisions cannot usually be undone.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise is a clustering algorithm that groups points in dense regions and labels sparse points as noise or outliers.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Clustering and anomaly detection.
cards.highLevel: It uses two parameters: epsilon neighborhood radius and minimum points. Points with enough neighbors become core points; connected core neighborhoods form clusters; isolated points become noise.
cards.whenUse: Use it when clusters have irregular shapes and you do not know the number of clusters, such as geospatial hotspots, sensor patterns, or spatial event clustering.
cards.limitations: It struggles when clusters have very different densities and in high-dimensional data where distance becomes less meaningful. Choosing epsilon can be difficult and scaling matters heavily.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: A probabilistic clustering model that represents data as a mixture of several Gaussian distributions, where each point has a probability of belonging to each component.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Clustering, density estimation, and soft assignment.
cards.highLevel: It usually uses expectation-maximization: estimate each point’s responsibility for each Gaussian, then update means, covariances, and mixture weights to maximize data likelihood.
cards.whenUse: Use it when clusters overlap and you want membership probabilities rather than hard assignments, such as customer segments with uncertainty or modeling continuous feature distributions.
cards.limitations: You must choose the number of components. It assumes Gaussian-shaped components, can be sensitive to initialization and outliers, and covariance estimation can be unstable with limited data.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: Principal Component Analysis is a linear dimensionality reduction method that finds directions of maximum variance and projects data onto fewer uncorrelated components.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Dimensionality reduction; sometimes preprocessing for classification, regression, clustering, or visualization.
cards.highLevel: It centers the data, computes directions that capture the most variance, and transforms each sample into coordinates along those directions. The first component captures the most variance, the second captures the next most, and so on.
cards.whenUse: Use it to compress numeric features, reduce noise, visualize high-dimensional data in 2D/3D, or remove multicollinearity before modeling.
cards.limitations: It is linear and variance-focused, so it may miss nonlinear structure or low-variance features that are predictive. Components can be hard to interpret and are sensitive to feature scaling.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding is a nonlinear visualization method that maps high-dimensional points into 2D or 3D while preserving local neighborhood relationships.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Dimensionality reduction for visualization, not usually for production feature compression.
cards.highLevel: It converts pairwise similarities in high-dimensional space and low-dimensional space into probabilities, then optimizes the map so nearby points remain nearby. The t-distribution helps separate clusters visually.
cards.whenUse: Use it to explore embeddings, image features, single-cell data, or document vectors and see whether similar items form visible neighborhoods.
cards.limitations: Global distances, cluster sizes, and gaps can be misleading. It is sensitive to perplexity, learning rate, random seed, and preprocessing, and it does not naturally transform new data without rerunning or approximations.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction method that often preserves both local neighborhoods and more global structure better than t-SNE.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Dimensionality reduction and visualization; sometimes used as preprocessing for clustering.
cards.highLevel: It builds a graph of nearest-neighbor relationships in high-dimensional space, then optimizes a low-dimensional layout that keeps connected points close while spreading unrelated points apart.
cards.whenUse: Use it for visualizing embeddings, biological measurements, text vectors, or image representations, especially when you need faster runtime than t-SNE or want a transform that can be applied to new points.
cards.limitations: Results depend on parameters such as neighbors and minimum distance. The visualization can still create apparent clusters that may not be statistically meaningful, and scaling/preprocessing strongly affects outcomes.

cards.heading: C. Unsupervised learning
cards.what: A set of techniques for identifying observations that are unusual compared with normal data, such as rare transactions, sensor failures, network intrusions, or abnormal patient measurements.
cards.learningType: Usually unsupervised or semi-supervised; can be supervised if labeled anomalies are available.
cards.taskType: Anomaly detection, sometimes framed as classification when labels exist.
cards.highLevel: Methods define normal behavior using density, distance, reconstruction error, isolation, statistical thresholds, or prediction residuals. Points that deviate strongly from the learned normal pattern receive high anomaly scores.
cards.whenUse: Use it when rare events matter and labeled examples are scarce: fraud screening, equipment fault detection, cybersecurity alerts, quality inspection, and monitoring data pipelines.
cards.limitations: Anomalies are context-dependent, rare labels make evaluation difficult, and many unusual points are harmless. Models can produce many false positives if thresholds and business costs are not carefully tuned.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: The proportion of predictions that are exactly correct among all predictions.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification metric.
cards.taskType: Classification.
cards.highLevel: It counts true positives and true negatives, divides by total examples, and returns one overall correctness rate.
cards.whenUse: Use it when classes are balanced and all mistakes have roughly similar cost, such as classifying equally common categories with no severe penalty difference.
cards.limitations: It is misleading on imbalanced data. A model predicting “not fraud” for every transaction may have high accuracy if fraud is rare, while being useless for fraud detection.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: A classification metric answering: of the examples the model predicted as positive, how many were actually positive?
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification metric.
cards.taskType: Classification, especially binary or one-vs-rest multiclass evaluation.
cards.highLevel: Precision equals true positives divided by all predicted positives. It focuses on the reliability of positive predictions and penalizes false alarms.
cards.whenUse: Use it when false positives are costly: flagging innocent users for fraud, sending expensive sales outreach, or alerting doctors about a condition that triggers invasive follow-up.
cards.limitations: High precision can be achieved by making very few positive predictions, so it must be considered with recall and business coverage. It depends on the chosen decision threshold.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: A classification metric answering: of all actual positive examples, how many did the model successfully find?
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification metric.
cards.taskType: Classification.
cards.highLevel: Recall equals true positives divided by actual positives. It focuses on missed positives and penalizes false negatives.
cards.whenUse: Use it when missing a positive case is costly: disease screening, safety defect detection, security threat detection, or identifying customers likely to churn before they leave.
cards.limitations: Maximizing recall can create many false positives. It should be balanced against precision, operational capacity, and the downstream cost of investigating alerts.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, producing one score that rewards models only when both false positives and false negatives are reasonably controlled.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification metric.
cards.taskType: Classification.
cards.highLevel: It combines precision and recall as 2 × precision × recall divided by precision + recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance between the two.
cards.whenUse: Use it for imbalanced classification when you need a single comparison metric and precision and recall are both important, such as spam detection or support-ticket escalation.
cards.limitations: It ignores true negatives and does not directly encode business costs. A model with the best F1 may not be the best after choosing an operating threshold or considering intervention capacity.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve measures how well a classifier ranks positives above negatives across all probability thresholds.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification metric.
cards.taskType: Classification, especially binary classification and ranking quality.
cards.highLevel: It plots true positive rate against false positive rate at many thresholds, then calculates the area under that curve. A value near 1 indicates strong ranking separation; 0.5 is close to random ranking.
cards.whenUse: Use it when comparing probabilistic classifiers independent of a single threshold, such as risk scoring models where users later choose different alert cutoffs.
cards.limitations: It can look strong under severe class imbalance even when precision is poor at practical thresholds. It also says little about calibration or exact business costs.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: A table that shows counts of predicted classes versus actual classes, making the types of classification mistakes visible.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification evaluation tool.
cards.taskType: Classification.
cards.highLevel: For binary classification it contains true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. For multiclass problems, each cell shows how often one actual class was predicted as another.
cards.whenUse: Use it to diagnose where a classifier fails: which disease is confused with another, which product category is mislabeled, or whether fraud alerts are dominated by false positives.
cards.limitations: It is count-based and threshold-dependent. Large classes can dominate the table, and it does not by itself provide costs, calibration, or ranking performance.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: Mean Absolute Error is a regression metric that averages the absolute size of prediction errors in the same units as the target.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised regression metric.
cards.taskType: Regression and forecasting.
cards.highLevel: For each example, subtract prediction from actual value, take the absolute value, and average across examples. Every unit of error contributes linearly.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you want an easy-to-interpret average error, such as “the model is off by 3.2 days” or “off by $500 on average.”
cards.limitations: It treats all errors linearly, so it may not penalize large mistakes enough when big misses are especially costly. It is not differentiable at zero, though this is rarely a practical issue for evaluation.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: Mean Squared Error is a regression metric that averages squared prediction errors, giving much more weight to large mistakes.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised regression metric and common training loss.
cards.taskType: Regression and forecasting.
cards.highLevel: It squares each residual before averaging, so errors of 10 count four times as much as errors of 5. This makes optimization mathematically convenient and sensitive to outliers.
cards.whenUse: Use it when large errors should be punished strongly, such as demand forecasting where big stockout errors are especially harmful, or when aligning evaluation with squared-error training.
cards.limitations: The units are squared target units, which are less intuitive. A few outliers can dominate the metric and make average performance look worse than typical performance.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: Root Mean Squared Error is the square root of MSE, returning error magnitude in the original target units while still penalizing large errors strongly.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised regression metric.
cards.taskType: Regression and forecasting.
cards.highLevel: It squares each error, averages the squared errors, then takes the square root. The squaring step emphasizes large misses; the square root restores units like dollars, days, or degrees.
cards.whenUse: Use it when stakeholders want error in natural units but large mistakes matter more than small mistakes, such as energy load forecasting or delivery-time prediction.
cards.limitations: It is still sensitive to outliers and may overstate typical error when the data has rare extreme values. It should often be reported alongside MAE or error percentiles.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: R-squared measures the fraction of target variance explained by a regression model compared with predicting the average target value.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised regression metric.
cards.taskType: Regression.
cards.highLevel: It compares the model’s residual sum of squares with the total sum of squares around the target mean. Higher values generally indicate better explanatory fit; values can be negative on test data.
cards.whenUse: Use it to communicate how much variation a model explains, especially in classical regression or when comparing models on the same dataset and target.
cards.limitations: It does not show error size in business units, can increase with irrelevant features on training data, and may be inappropriate for nonlinear goals, time-series leakage, or highly noisy targets.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: Log loss measures the quality of predicted class probabilities, heavily penalizing confident predictions that are wrong.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised classification metric and training loss.
cards.taskType: Classification, especially probabilistic binary or multiclass classification.
cards.highLevel: For each example, it takes the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the true class and averages across examples. A confident wrong prediction receives a very large penalty.
cards.whenUse: Use it when probability calibration matters, such as risk scoring, bidding, medical triage, or any workflow where predicted probabilities drive decisions rather than only class labels.
cards.limitations: It can be hard to interpret for nontechnical audiences. It is sensitive to mislabeled data and can punish overconfident models harshly even if their class predictions are often correct.

cards.heading: D. Model evaluation
cards.what: An evaluation procedure that repeatedly trains and validates models across different data folds to estimate how stable performance is.
cards.learningType: Not a model; it is a supervised evaluation method.
cards.taskType: Classification and regression evaluation; with specialized metrics it can also help select unsupervised settings.
cards.highLevel: The dataset is split into several folds. Each fold becomes validation once while the remaining folds train the model, and the resulting scores are averaged with variance or confidence intervals.
cards.whenUse: Use it to compare model families, tune hyperparameters, or report more reliable performance when one holdout set is too small or too dependent on random splitting.
cards.limitations: It multiplies training time and can leak information if preprocessing is not fitted inside each training fold. Time-series, grouped, and patient-level data require specialized folds.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A basic computational unit in a neural network that takes input numbers, combines them using weights and a bias, then passes the result through an activation function.
cards.learningType: Part of supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning models depending on the training objective.
cards.taskType: Can support classification, regression, clustering-like representation learning, dimensionality reduction, generation, and sequence modeling.
cards.highLevel: A neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs, adds a bias, and applies a nonlinear activation such as ReLU or sigmoid. Many neurons connected in layers can approximate complex functions.
cards.whenUse: Use neural-network neurons when raw feature interactions are complex, such as pixels in images, words in text, signals in audio, or nonlinear patterns in large tabular data.
cards.limitations: Individual neurons are usually not easily interpretable. Networks with many neurons require data, compute, careful regularization, and monitoring for overfitting or unstable training.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: Trainable parameters that determine how strongly each input or previous neuron influences the next neuron’s output.
cards.learningType: Used inside neural models trained with supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, or reinforcement objectives.
cards.taskType: Applies to any neural-network task type.
cards.highLevel: During training, backpropagation calculates how changing each weight would affect the loss, and the optimizer updates weights in directions that reduce the loss.
cards.whenUse: Use the concept to understand what a neural network learns: image filters in CNNs, token interactions in transformers, or coefficients in a simple dense layer.
cards.limitations: Weights are numerous and distributed, so direct human interpretation is difficult. Poor initialization, too-large updates, or insufficient regularization can make weights unstable or cause overfitting.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A trainable offset added to a neuron’s weighted input, allowing the activation threshold to shift instead of forcing outputs to pass through the origin.
cards.learningType: Used inside neural models across training paradigms.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, representation learning, and generative tasks.
cards.highLevel: After multiplying inputs by weights, the neuron adds a bias term before the activation. This lets the model represent patterns even when all inputs are zero or when a boundary needs to move.
cards.whenUse: Use it as a standard part of dense, convolutional, and recurrent layers when you want flexible function approximation.
cards.limitations: Bias terms can still contribute to overfitting, and in some architectures they may be redundant with normalization layers. They are not the same as social or data bias.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A nonlinear function applied inside neural networks so stacked layers can learn complex nonlinear relationships rather than collapsing into one linear transformation.
cards.learningType: Used inside models trained under many paradigms.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, representation learning, sequence modeling, and generation.
cards.highLevel: The activation transforms a neuron’s pre-activation value. ReLU keeps positive values and zeros negatives; sigmoid maps to 0–1; tanh maps to -1–1; GELU is common in transformers.
cards.whenUse: Use ReLU/GELU-like activations for most hidden layers, sigmoid for binary probabilities, and softmax for multiclass output probabilities.
cards.limitations: Poor choices can cause vanishing gradients, dead neurons, slow training, or poorly calibrated outputs. Output activations must match the loss and target type.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A mathematical objective that measures how bad a model’s predictions are relative to the training target or objective.
cards.learningType: Used in supervised, self-supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning with different definitions of error or reward.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, generative modeling, representation learning, and control.
cards.highLevel: The model produces predictions, the loss function converts prediction quality into a number, and optimization updates parameters to reduce that number. Examples include cross-entropy for classification and MSE for regression.
cards.whenUse: Use a loss that matches the business and statistical goal: log loss for probabilities, MAE/MSE for numeric prediction, contrastive loss for embeddings, or reconstruction loss for autoencoders.
cards.limitations: Optimizing the wrong loss can improve a metric that does not matter in practice. Loss values may be hard to compare across datasets and can be distorted by label noise or class imbalance.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: An algorithm that updates model parameters during training based on gradients from the loss function.
cards.learningType: Used across neural learning paradigms.
cards.taskType: Applies to all neural-network task types.
cards.highLevel: The optimizer calculates parameter updates using gradients and settings such as learning rate, momentum, or adaptive per-parameter scaling. Common optimizers include SGD, Adam, AdamW, and RMSProp.
cards.whenUse: Use Adam or AdamW for many deep-learning defaults, SGD with momentum when carefully tuning vision models, and specialized optimizers for very large models or constrained hardware.
cards.limitations: Optimizers introduce hyperparameters that strongly affect convergence. A poor choice can make training slow, unstable, overfit, or converge to a worse solution.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A core optimization method that adjusts parameters in the direction that most reduces the loss according to calculated gradients.
cards.learningType: Optimization technique used in supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, representation learning, and generative modeling.
cards.highLevel: It computes the slope of the loss with respect to each parameter and takes a step in the opposite direction. Mini-batch gradient descent estimates gradients using a subset of training examples for efficiency.
cards.whenUse: Use it whenever training differentiable models such as linear models, logistic regression, neural networks, and many embedding models.
cards.limitations: It can get stuck in poor regions, diverge if the learning rate is too high, train slowly if too low, and be affected by noisy gradients or poorly scaled features.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: The algorithm used to efficiently compute gradients for all parameters in a neural network by applying the chain rule from the output layer back to earlier layers.
cards.learningType: Training algorithm used across neural learning paradigms.
cards.taskType: Applies to neural classification, regression, sequence modeling, representation learning, and generation.
cards.highLevel: After a forward pass computes predictions and loss, backpropagation works backward through the network, calculating how each weight contributed to the loss. The optimizer then updates parameters.
cards.whenUse: Use it to train multilayer neural networks, from simple MLPs to CNNs, RNNs, transformers, autoencoders, and diffusion models.
cards.limitations: Gradients can vanish, explode, or become noisy. Some operations are not differentiable, and memory use can be high because intermediate activations must be stored for the backward pass.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A hyperparameter controlling how large each optimizer update is during training.
cards.learningType: Training hyperparameter across ML models optimized by gradient methods.
cards.taskType: Applies to neural classification, regression, representation learning, and generative models.
cards.highLevel: At each step, gradients are multiplied by the learning rate before parameters are updated. Schedules may decrease the rate over time or warm it up at the start.
cards.whenUse: Tune it when training is unstable, too slow, or stuck. Learning-rate schedules are especially important for deep networks and transformer training.
cards.limitations: Too high a learning rate can cause divergence or bouncing around good solutions; too low can make training painfully slow or stuck in suboptimal regions. Best values depend on batch size, optimizer, and architecture.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: An epoch is one complete pass through the training dataset during model training.
cards.learningType: Training concept, not a model.
cards.taskType: Applies to any task trained iteratively, especially deep learning.
cards.highLevel: If a dataset has 10,000 examples and the batch size is 100, one epoch contains 100 parameter-update steps. Multiple epochs let the model revisit data and refine parameters.
cards.whenUse: Use epochs to control how long training runs. Monitor training and validation loss across epochs to decide whether to continue, stop early, or adjust regularization.
cards.limitations: Too few epochs can underfit; too many can overfit or waste compute. Epoch counts are not comparable across datasets with different sizes, augmentation, batch sizes, or optimizers.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: The number of training examples processed before the model performs one parameter update.
cards.learningType: Training hyperparameter, not a model.
cards.taskType: Applies to neural classification, regression, generation, and representation learning.
cards.highLevel: Mini-batch training estimates the gradient from a batch rather than the full dataset. Smaller batches give noisier but frequent updates; larger batches give smoother gradients and better hardware utilization.
cards.whenUse: Tune it based on GPU memory, training stability, and speed. Larger batches are common for large models, while smaller batches can help generalization or fit limited hardware.
cards.limitations: Very small batches can make training noisy and slow; very large batches may require learning-rate adjustment and can generalize worse. Hardware limits often constrain the choice.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A regularization technique that randomly disables a fraction of neurons or activations during training to reduce co-adaptation and overfitting.
cards.learningType: Training technique used in neural models across supervised and self-supervised tasks.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, sequence modeling, and representation learning.
cards.highLevel: During each training step, selected activations are set to zero. At inference, all units are used with scaled activations, making the model behave like an average of many thinner networks.
cards.whenUse: Use it in neural networks when validation loss worsens while training loss keeps improving, especially in dense layers or smaller datasets.
cards.limitations: Too much dropout slows learning and can underfit. It is less commonly needed in some modern architectures with normalization, large datasets, data augmentation, or strong weight decay.

cards.heading: E. Deep learning basics
cards.what: A layer that normalizes intermediate activations within a mini-batch and learns scale and shift parameters, often making deep networks easier and faster to train.
cards.learningType: Neural-network training component, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Applies to classification, regression, and representation learning, especially in CNNs and MLPs.
cards.highLevel: For each mini-batch, it standardizes activations using batch mean and variance, then applies learned scale and offset. Running statistics are used during inference.
cards.whenUse: Use it in deep feedforward or convolutional networks to stabilize training, allow higher learning rates, and reduce sensitivity to initialization.
cards.limitations: It behaves differently during training and inference, can be unreliable with very small batch sizes, and is less natural for variable-length sequences where layer normalization is often preferred.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A multilayer perceptron is a feedforward neural network made of fully connected layers where each neuron connects to every output from the previous layer.
cards.learningType: Can be trained supervised, unsupervised, or self-supervised depending on objective.
cards.taskType: Classification and regression most commonly; also feature learning and tabular deep learning.
cards.highLevel: Input features pass through one or more dense layers with nonlinear activations. The final layer produces class probabilities, numeric predictions, or embeddings depending on the task.
cards.whenUse: Use it for tabular data baselines, simple nonlinear modeling, embedding transformations, or as the prediction head on top of pretrained features.
cards.limitations: It ignores spatial and sequence structure unless manually encoded. It can overfit tabular data, require scaling, and often underperform tree-based models on small structured datasets.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A convolutional neural network is designed to process grid-like data such as images by learning local filters that detect patterns like edges, textures, and shapes.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification, regression, object detection, segmentation, feature extraction, and image generation components.
cards.highLevel: Convolutional filters slide across the input and share weights across locations. Early layers detect simple local patterns; deeper layers combine them into larger objects or semantic features.
cards.whenUse: Use it for images, medical scans, satellite imagery, video frames, spectrograms, and other data where local spatial patterns matter.
cards.limitations: It needs substantial data or transfer learning, can be sensitive to distribution shifts, and may miss long-range relationships unless combined with attention or deeper architectures.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A recurrent neural network processes sequences by maintaining a hidden state that is updated step by step as each element is read.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised depending on the sequence objective.
cards.taskType: Sequence classification, regression, forecasting, language modeling, and sequence generation.
cards.highLevel: At each time step, the network combines the current input with the previous hidden state, allowing earlier information to influence later predictions.
cards.whenUse: Use it for simple sequential patterns such as sensor streams, short text sequences, or time-series baselines when sequence order matters.
cards.limitations: Plain RNNs struggle with long-term dependencies because gradients vanish or explode. They are slower to parallelize than transformers and have largely been replaced by LSTMs, GRUs, or attention models for many tasks.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: Long Short-Term Memory is a recurrent architecture designed to remember information over longer sequences using gated memory cells.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised.
cards.taskType: Sequence classification, sequence regression, forecasting, speech, text, and time-series modeling.
cards.highLevel: It uses input, forget, and output gates to decide what information to store, erase, and expose from its memory cell at each time step. This helps reduce vanishing-gradient problems.
cards.whenUse: Use it for time-series forecasting, speech features, event sequences, and text tasks when data is sequential and transformers are too large or unnecessary.
cards.limitations: It is slower to train than parallel attention models, can still struggle with very long contexts, and has more parameters and complexity than GRUs or simple RNNs.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: Gated Recurrent Unit is a simpler gated recurrent architecture that combines some LSTM ideas with fewer gates and parameters.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised.
cards.taskType: Sequence classification, regression, forecasting, and sequence modeling.
cards.highLevel: It uses update and reset gates to control how much past information is retained or replaced. This helps model dependencies while being lighter than an LSTM.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you need recurrent modeling but want faster training or fewer parameters than LSTM, such as moderate-length time-series or embedded sequence models.
cards.limitations: It may be less expressive than LSTM for some tasks and still lacks the parallelism and long-context handling of transformers.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A neural network trained to compress input data into a latent representation and reconstruct the original input from that compressed code.
cards.learningType: Usually unsupervised or self-supervised.
cards.taskType: Dimensionality reduction, representation learning, denoising, anomaly detection, and generative modeling variants.
cards.highLevel: An encoder maps input to a lower-dimensional latent space; a decoder reconstructs the input. Training minimizes reconstruction error or a related objective.
cards.whenUse: Use it to learn compressed features, denoise images/signals, detect anomalies via high reconstruction error, or initialize representations when labels are limited.
cards.limitations: A standard autoencoder may simply learn an identity-like mapping if too powerful. Latent dimensions can be hard to interpret, and low reconstruction error does not always mean useful features.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A neural architecture based on attention mechanisms that can model relationships between all elements in a sequence without processing them strictly one at a time.
cards.learningType: Commonly self-supervised for pretraining, then supervised or reinforcement-tuned for downstream use.
cards.taskType: NLP, classification, regression on sequences, generation, translation, summarization, retrieval embeddings, vision, audio, and multimodal tasks.
cards.highLevel: It represents tokens as embeddings, adds position information, and uses self-attention layers to let each token weigh information from other tokens. Feedforward layers and normalization refine the representations.
cards.whenUse: Use it for language models, translation, document understanding, code generation, image patches, multimodal systems, and any task where long-range interactions are important.
cards.limitations: It can require large data and compute, context length is finite, and attention cost grows with sequence length. Outputs can still be biased, hallucinated, or poorly calibrated.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: An architecture with one network component that encodes an input into internal representations and another component that decodes those representations into an output sequence.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised depending on task.
cards.taskType: Sequence-to-sequence generation, translation, summarization, speech recognition, image captioning, and structured output prediction.
cards.highLevel: The encoder reads the source input and builds contextual representations. The decoder generates the output step by step, often attending to encoder states and previously generated output tokens.
cards.whenUse: Use it when input and output are different sequences: translate English to Swedish, summarize an article, convert speech to text, or answer questions from a passage.
cards.limitations: Training and inference can be expensive, and generated outputs may be factually wrong or repetitive. Autoregressive decoding is slower because tokens are produced sequentially.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A generative adversarial network contains a generator that creates synthetic examples and a discriminator that tries to distinguish real examples from generated ones.
cards.learningType: Unsupervised or self-supervised generative learning.
cards.taskType: Generative modeling, image synthesis, data augmentation, style transfer, and representation learning.
cards.highLevel: The generator and discriminator train in competition. The generator improves by fooling the discriminator; the discriminator improves by detecting fakes. Ideally, generated samples become realistic.
cards.whenUse: Use it for realistic image generation, super-resolution, domain translation, synthetic data experiments, or creative generation when sharp outputs are valuable.
cards.limitations: GAN training is unstable, sensitive to architecture and hyperparameters, and can suffer mode collapse where the generator produces limited varieties. Evaluation is difficult.

cards.heading: F. Neural network architectures
cards.what: A generative model that learns to create data by reversing a gradual noise-adding process, commonly used for high-quality image, audio, video, and 3D generation.
cards.learningType: Self-supervised generative learning.
cards.taskType: Generative AI rather than classification/regression, though diffusion backbones can be conditioned on labels, text, or images.
cards.highLevel: Training corrupts real data with noise at different levels and teaches a neural network to predict or remove that noise. Generation starts from random noise and iteratively denoises it into a sample.
cards.whenUse: Use it for text-to-image generation, image editing, inpainting, super-resolution, video generation, molecular design, and other tasks where diverse high-fidelity samples are needed.
cards.limitations: Sampling can be slower than one-pass models, compute requirements are high, and outputs may reflect training-data biases or fail prompt details. Controlling exact structure can be difficult.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: The process of converting raw text into smaller units called tokens, such as words, subwords, characters, or byte-level pieces, so language models can process text numerically.
cards.learningType: Preprocessing step, not supervised or unsupervised by itself.
cards.taskType: Used before NLP classification, regression, clustering, search, translation, summarization, and generation.
cards.highLevel: A tokenizer applies rules or a learned vocabulary to split text and map each token to an integer ID. Modern LLMs commonly use subword tokenization so rare words can be represented as combinations of common pieces.
cards.whenUse: Use it in any NLP pipeline: sentiment analysis, document search, machine translation, chatbots, text classification, or LLM prompting.
cards.limitations: Tokenization affects cost, context length, multilingual performance, and handling of rare words. Poor tokenization can split names, numbers, code, or non-English text in ways that hurt model behavior.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: Dense numeric vectors that represent words, sentences, documents, users, items, or other objects so similar meanings or behaviors are close in vector space.
cards.learningType: Often learned through self-supervised or supervised objectives; used in both supervised and unsupervised workflows.
cards.taskType: Classification, clustering, semantic search, recommendation, dimensionality reduction, and retrieval.
cards.highLevel: A model maps each object to a vector. Training encourages related objects to have nearby vectors, using objectives such as context prediction, contrastive learning, or next-token prediction.
cards.whenUse: Use embeddings when raw IDs or text need semantic representation: search by meaning, cluster documents, recommend similar products, or feed pretrained language features into a classifier.
cards.limitations: Embedding similarity is not perfect truth. Vectors can encode bias, become stale as language or products change, and perform poorly outside the domain they were trained on.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: Information added to token embeddings so a transformer knows the order or position of tokens, since attention alone does not inherently encode sequence order.
cards.learningType: Model component, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Used in sequence classification, generation, translation, summarization, and other transformer tasks.
cards.highLevel: Positions can be represented with fixed sinusoidal patterns, learned position embeddings, rotary embeddings, or relative position schemes. These are combined with token embeddings before or during attention.
cards.whenUse: Use it whenever a transformer processes ordered data such as text, code, time series, audio frames, or image patches arranged in sequence.
cards.limitations: Position schemes can limit maximum context length or generalization to longer sequences. Some methods extrapolate poorly beyond the lengths seen during training.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: A mechanism that lets a model focus on the most relevant parts of an input when creating a representation or generating an output.
cards.learningType: Model component used in supervised, self-supervised, and generative learning.
cards.taskType: NLP classification, translation, summarization, generation, retrieval, vision, and multimodal tasks.
cards.highLevel: The model creates query, key, and value vectors. Attention scores compare queries with keys, then use the scores to compute weighted combinations of values, allowing context-dependent information flow.
cards.whenUse: Use attention when relationships between distant elements matter, such as linking pronouns to nouns, aligning translation phrases, or connecting an image region to a caption word.
cards.limitations: Attention can be expensive for long sequences and is not always a faithful explanation of model reasoning. It can focus on spurious correlations if training data encourages them.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: A form of attention where each token in a sequence attends to other tokens in the same sequence to build context-aware representations.
cards.learningType: Model component used mainly in self-supervised and supervised transformer training.
cards.taskType: NLP generation, classification, translation, summarization, code modeling, vision transformers, and multimodal tasks.
cards.highLevel: Every token produces a query, key, and value. The token compares its query with all keys, then combines values from relevant positions, allowing words to incorporate context from surrounding words.
cards.whenUse: Use it when a model must understand relationships across a sequence, such as subject-verb agreement, long-distance dependencies, or interactions between document sections.
cards.limitations: Standard self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, making long documents expensive. It also needs positional information to distinguish order.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: A transformer component that runs several attention mechanisms in parallel so the model can capture different relationship types at the same time.
cards.learningType: Model component used in transformer-based learning.
cards.taskType: Sequence classification, generation, translation, summarization, vision, and multimodal modeling.
cards.highLevel: Each head learns separate query, key, and value projections and attends differently. Outputs from all heads are concatenated and transformed, giving the layer multiple perspectives on the same sequence.
cards.whenUse: Use it as a standard part of transformer encoders and decoders when relationships may involve syntax, semantics, position, coreference, or formatting simultaneously.
cards.limitations: More heads increase compute and memory. Some heads can be redundant, and interpreting what each head does is not always straightforward.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: In NLP transformers, an encoder reads the full input sequence and produces contextual representations for each token.
cards.learningType: Usually pretrained self-supervised and fine-tuned supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification, token labeling, semantic search embeddings, extractive question answering, and representation learning.
cards.highLevel: Encoder self-attention can usually look at all tokens in the input at once, creating bidirectional context. The final representations are then pooled or used by task-specific heads.
cards.whenUse: Use encoders for understanding tasks: sentiment classification, named entity recognition, document ranking, semantic similarity, or extracting answers from a passage.
cards.limitations: Encoders are not naturally designed for open-ended autoregressive generation. Input length is limited, and fine-tuned encoders can be sensitive to domain shift.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: In transformer language models, a decoder generates output tokens autoregressively, usually predicting the next token from previous tokens.
cards.learningType: Usually self-supervised during pretraining and supervised or preference-tuned later.
cards.taskType: Text generation, code generation, chat, summarization, translation in decoder-only setups, and sequence completion.
cards.highLevel: Causal self-attention masks future tokens so each position can only attend to earlier positions. The model repeatedly predicts the next token, appends it, and continues.
cards.whenUse: Use decoders for generative tasks such as chatbots, writing assistance, code completion, creative text generation, and tool-using agents.
cards.limitations: Generation is sequential and can be slow for long outputs. The model may hallucinate, repeat, or produce unsafe/biased content without proper controls and evaluation.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers is an encoder-only transformer family pretrained to understand text using bidirectional context.
cards.learningType: Pretrained self-supervised; commonly fine-tuned supervised.
cards.taskType: Classification, token classification, semantic similarity, retrieval, and extractive question answering.
cards.highLevel: BERT is pretrained with objectives such as masked language modeling, where some tokens are hidden and the model learns to predict them from both left and right context. Fine-tuning adds a task-specific head.
cards.whenUse: Use BERT-style models for NLP understanding tasks: sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, legal/medical document classification, or ranking passages for search.
cards.limitations: Classic BERT is not ideal for long documents or open-ended generation. It has fixed context limits and may need domain-specific fine-tuning for specialized vocabulary.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: Generative Pretrained Transformer refers to decoder-only transformer language models trained primarily to predict the next token and generate text or code.
cards.learningType: Self-supervised pretraining, often followed by supervised instruction tuning and preference optimization.
cards.taskType: Text generation, chat, summarization, code generation, reasoning assistance, classification through prompting, and tool use.
cards.highLevel: The model reads previous tokens through causal self-attention and learns probability distributions over the next token. During generation, it samples or selects tokens repeatedly to form an output.
cards.whenUse: Use GPT-style models for drafting, conversation, code assistance, summarization, extraction, brainstorming, and natural-language interfaces over tools or data.
cards.limitations: They can hallucinate, be sensitive to prompt wording, have finite context windows, and may reproduce biases or outdated information from training data. They require evaluation and guardrails for high-stakes use.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
