cards.what: A modeling setup where an input sequence is transformed into an output sequence, often with different lengths and vocabularies.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised depending on available pairs and objective.
cards.taskType: Translation, summarization, speech recognition, question answering, code translation, and structured text generation.
cards.highLevel: An encoder reads the source sequence, and a decoder generates the target sequence token by token, often using attention to reference relevant source positions.
cards.whenUse: Use it when the task naturally maps one ordered input to another ordered output, such as French-to-English translation, article-to-summary, or audio-to-transcript.
cards.limitations: It needs high-quality paired training data for supervised tasks. Outputs can omit details, hallucinate, or degrade on long inputs and rare domain terminology.

cards.heading: G. NLP and transformers
cards.what: A technique that hides certain tokens or blocks attention to control what information a model can see during training or generation.
cards.learningType: Training/modeling technique, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Used in language-model pretraining, sequence generation, classification, and attention control.
cards.highLevel: In masked language modeling, selected tokens are replaced and predicted from context. In causal masking, future tokens are hidden so a decoder predicts only from previous tokens. Padding masks prevent attention to filler positions.
cards.whenUse: Use masking to train BERT-like models, build GPT-style causal generation, handle padded batches, or prevent a model from seeing future information in forecasting.
cards.limitations: Incorrect masking causes leakage or prevents useful context. Masking strategy strongly affects what a model learns and can create mismatch between training and inference.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: The initial large-scale training phase where a model learns general language, code, image, or multimodal patterns from massive datasets before being adapted to specific tasks.
cards.learningType: Usually self-supervised.
cards.taskType: Foundation for generation, classification, embeddings, retrieval, summarization, translation, and many downstream tasks.
cards.highLevel: The model optimizes a broad objective such as next-token prediction, masked-token prediction, contrastive learning, or denoising over huge corpora. It learns reusable representations and world/language patterns.
cards.whenUse: Use pretrained models instead of training from scratch when building NLP, vision, audio, or multimodal applications. Pretraining gives strong general ability that can be fine-tuned or prompted.
cards.limitations: It is expensive and may absorb biases, private information, copyrighted material, or outdated facts from training data. Pretraining alone does not guarantee instruction following or factual reliability.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: The process of continuing training of a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific or domain-specific dataset to adapt its behavior.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised, self-supervised, or preference-based depending on data.
cards.taskType: Classification, generation, extraction, summarization, domain adaptation, and style control.
cards.highLevel: Starting from pretrained weights, training updates some or all parameters using examples relevant to the target task. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA update small adapter weights instead of the full model.
cards.whenUse: Use it when prompting is not enough, when you need consistent format/style, domain terminology, task specialization, or better performance on proprietary examples.
cards.limitations: Fine-tuning needs representative data and evaluation. It can overfit, forget general abilities, amplify dataset errors, and is not the best way to add frequently changing factual knowledge compared with retrieval.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: A fine-tuning stage where a model learns to follow natural-language instructions by training on prompt-response examples.
cards.learningType: Supervised fine-tuning on instruction datasets.
cards.taskType: Improves general task following for generation, extraction, summarization, classification by prompting, and chat.
cards.highLevel: The model sees many examples of user instructions paired with desired responses. Training encourages it to map diverse requests to helpful, structured, and task-aligned outputs.
cards.whenUse: Use it when turning a base language model into an assistant, enterprise helper, coding assistant, or model that reliably follows formatting and task instructions.
cards.limitations: It depends on the quality and diversity of instruction data. It can teach superficial compliance without deep factuality, and may not cover specialized tasks unless examples are included.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback is a training approach that uses human preferences to make model outputs more helpful, safe, or aligned with user expectations.
cards.learningType: Reinforcement/preference optimization after supervised or self-supervised training.
cards.taskType: Mainly improves generative assistant behavior rather than a standard classification/regression task.
cards.highLevel: Humans compare model responses, a reward model learns those preferences, and the language model is optimized to produce outputs that score higher under the reward model, often with constraints to avoid drifting too far.
cards.whenUse: Use it for chatbots and assistants where raw next-token prediction gives fluent but unhelpful or unsafe behavior. It helps models refuse harmful requests, follow instructions, and produce preferred styles.
cards.limitations: Human preferences can be inconsistent, culturally narrow, or gamed by the model. RLHF can make models overly cautious, verbose, or optimized for pleasing answers rather than truth.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: The practice of designing instructions, context, examples, constraints, and output formats to guide a language model’s behavior without changing its weights.
cards.learningType: Not supervised or unsupervised; it is an inference-time control technique.
cards.taskType: Used for generation, extraction, classification-by-prompt, summarization, reasoning workflows, and tool use.
cards.highLevel: You provide clear task instructions, relevant context, examples, role definitions, formatting requirements, and sometimes step-by-step decomposition. The model conditions its next-token generation on the prompt.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you need quick adaptation, structured outputs, few-shot examples, or task orchestration without training. It is often the first approach before fine-tuning.
cards.limitations: Prompts can be brittle, model-specific, and vulnerable to prompt injection when external text is included. Prompting cannot reliably add missing model knowledge or guarantee correctness.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: Vector representations produced by an embedding model to capture semantic meaning of text, images, code, users, products, or other objects in a way that supports similarity search.
cards.learningType: Usually learned through self-supervised, contrastive, or supervised objectives; used in retrieval and downstream ML.
cards.taskType: Semantic search, clustering, recommendation, classification features, retrieval-augmented generation, and dimensionality reduction.
cards.highLevel: An embedding model maps input content into a fixed-length vector. Similar items should have nearby vectors under cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance.
cards.whenUse: Use embeddings in RAG systems to retrieve relevant documents for a question, find duplicate support tickets, recommend similar products, or cluster documents by topic.
cards.limitations: Similarity depends on the embedding model and training domain. Embeddings can miss exact facts, numbers, negation, or rare terms, and they must be refreshed when source content changes.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: A database or indexing system optimized for storing embeddings and performing fast nearest-neighbor similarity search at scale.
cards.learningType: Infrastructure component, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Supports semantic search, RAG, recommendation, clustering workflows, and retrieval features.
cards.highLevel: It stores vectors plus metadata, builds approximate nearest-neighbor indexes, and returns items whose vectors are closest to a query vector. Metadata filters can restrict search by date, source, tenant, or permission.
cards.whenUse: Use it when you need fast semantic retrieval over many documents, products, images, or user profiles, especially for RAG chatbots and recommendation systems.
cards.limitations: Approximate search may miss some true nearest neighbors, and poor chunking or embeddings reduce quality. Access control, freshness, duplicate handling, and metadata design are critical in production.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: Search based on meaning rather than exact keyword overlap, typically using embeddings to retrieve items conceptually related to a query.
cards.learningType: Usually uses self-supervised embeddings; the search process itself is not supervised unless trained with relevance labels.
cards.taskType: Retrieval, recommendation, clustering support, and RAG.
cards.highLevel: The query and documents are embedded into the same vector space. The system retrieves documents with high vector similarity and may combine this with keyword search, filters, or reranking.
cards.whenUse: Use it when users ask natural-language questions and relevant documents may use different wording, such as finding “refund policy” content when the document says “returns and reimbursements.”
cards.limitations: It can retrieve semantically similar but factually wrong or outdated content. It may underperform for exact identifiers, numbers, names, and rare keywords unless combined with lexical search.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a pattern where a language model retrieves relevant external information and uses it as context when generating an answer.
cards.learningType: System pattern combining retrieval with generative modeling; usually uses self-supervised pretrained models and sometimes supervised rerankers.
cards.taskType: Question answering, summarization, enterprise search, grounded chatbots, support assistants, and knowledge-base interfaces.
cards.highLevel: A user query is transformed into a search query or embedding, relevant chunks are retrieved, optionally reranked, and inserted into the prompt. The LLM answers using that retrieved context.
cards.whenUse: Use it when answers depend on private, current, or large document collections that should not be memorized in model weights, such as company policies, product docs, or customer support articles.
cards.limitations: Quality depends on retrieval, chunking, permissions, freshness, and prompt design. RAG can still hallucinate if retrieved context is missing, conflicting, or ignored by the model.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: The process of splitting documents into smaller pieces for indexing and retrieval in search or RAG systems.
cards.learningType: Preprocessing technique, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Supports semantic search, RAG, summarization, and document classification workflows.
cards.highLevel: Documents are divided by paragraphs, headings, token windows, semantic boundaries, or overlaps. Each chunk is embedded and stored with metadata so relevant sections can be retrieved later.
cards.whenUse: Use it when documents are too long for embedding models or LLM context windows. Good chunking helps retrieve the exact policy paragraph, code section, or support answer needed.
cards.limitations: Chunks that are too small lose context; chunks that are too large dilute relevance. Overlap increases recall but adds cost and duplicates. Tables, code, and PDFs need special handling.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: A second-stage retrieval step that reorders initially retrieved candidates using a more accurate model that directly scores query-document relevance.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised or self-supervised ranking model; infrastructure step in retrieval systems.
cards.taskType: Retrieval, semantic search, RAG, recommendation, and ranking.
cards.highLevel: A fast first-stage retriever returns many candidate chunks. A reranker then evaluates each query-candidate pair more carefully, often with a cross-encoder, and sorts the best evidence to the top.
cards.whenUse: Use it when vector search returns roughly relevant results but the top few are not precise enough for answering, especially in enterprise RAG and support search.
cards.limitations: Reranking adds latency and cost because it scores candidates individually. It cannot recover documents missing from the first-stage retrieval set, so recall still matters.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: A model output that is fluent or confident but unsupported, incorrect, fabricated, or inconsistent with the provided context.
cards.learningType: Failure mode of generative models, not a learning type.
cards.taskType: Relevant to generation, question answering, summarization, extraction, and RAG systems.
cards.highLevel: Language models generate likely text based on patterns, not guaranteed truth. If knowledge is missing, context is weak, or the prompt rewards completeness over uncertainty, the model may invent details.
cards.whenUse: Track it whenever LLM outputs affect decisions, documentation, customer communication, legal/medical/financial workflows, or data extraction from sources.
cards.limitations: Hallucinations cannot be eliminated by prompting alone. Mitigation requires retrieval, citations, constrained decoding, validation, abstention behavior, human review, and task-specific evaluation.

cards.heading: H. LLM and RAG
cards.what: The process of measuring whether an LLM or RAG system produces correct, useful, safe, grounded, and appropriately formatted outputs.
cards.learningType: Evaluation practice, not a model.
cards.taskType: Applies to generation, retrieval, classification-by-prompt, summarization, extraction, and agent workflows.
cards.highLevel: Evaluation can include human review, benchmark datasets, automated checks, retrieval metrics, factuality/groundedness scoring, pairwise preference tests, regression tests, and production monitoring.
cards.whenUse: Use it before deploying LLM systems and whenever prompts, models, retrieval indexes, or documents change. Create test sets with realistic user questions and expected evidence.
cards.limitations: Automated LLM-as-judge scores can be biased or inconsistent. Benchmarks may not match your domain, and evaluating open-ended answers is harder than evaluating fixed-label classification.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: A reproducible sequence of data processing, feature engineering, training, evaluation, and deployment steps that turns raw data into model outputs.
cards.learningType: Engineering concept used for supervised, unsupervised, and generative systems.
cards.taskType: Supports all task types by organizing preprocessing, model training, validation, and inference.
cards.highLevel: A pipeline chains steps such as cleaning, encoding, scaling, feature creation, model fitting, prediction, and postprocessing. In production, the same transformations must run consistently during training and inference.
cards.whenUse: Use pipelines to avoid manual notebooks becoming fragile workflows, to prevent train-serving skew, and to make experiments repeatable across teams and environments.
cards.limitations: Pipelines can become complex and hard to debug if not modular. Hidden state, version mismatches, or inconsistent preprocessing can cause silent production errors.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: Data preparation steps performed before modeling, such as cleaning missing values, encoding categories, scaling numbers, normalizing text, resizing images, or creating train/test-safe transformations.
cards.learningType: Not a learning paradigm; used across ML workflows.
cards.taskType: Supports classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, forecasting, and generation.
cards.highLevel: Preprocessing converts raw, messy data into representations suitable for algorithms. Some transformations are fitted on training data, such as scalers or imputers, then applied unchanged to validation/test/production data.
cards.whenUse: Use it whenever raw data has missing values, inconsistent units, categories, outliers, text formatting issues, image size differences, or features that models cannot directly consume.
cards.limitations: Bad preprocessing can leak test information, erase useful signal, amplify bias, or create mismatches between training and production. The right steps depend on model type and data semantics.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: A system for defining, storing, versioning, and serving ML features consistently for training and online inference.
cards.learningType: Infrastructure component, not supervised or unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Supports classification, regression, recommendation, ranking, forecasting, and personalization systems.
cards.highLevel: Feature definitions compute reusable variables from raw data, store historical values for training, and serve fresh values with low latency for predictions. Metadata tracks ownership, freshness, and lineage.
cards.whenUse: Use it when multiple models reuse features, when online and offline feature consistency matters, or when real-time prediction needs fast access to current user or item attributes.
cards.limitations: Feature stores add operational complexity. Poorly designed features can still leak future data, become stale, or be misused across teams. They require governance and monitoring.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: The practice of recording model runs, parameters, code versions, datasets, metrics, artifacts, and notes so experiments can be compared and reproduced.
cards.learningType: Engineering practice, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Supports every ML task type.
cards.highLevel: Each training run logs configuration, random seeds, dataset versions, model artifacts, evaluation metrics, and sometimes plots or predictions. Tools can compare runs and register promising models.
cards.whenUse: Use it whenever you try multiple models, hyperparameters, features, prompts, or datasets. It prevents losing the details behind the “best” result.
cards.limitations: It only helps if teams log meaningful metadata consistently. Large artifacts can be costly, and metrics can still be misleading if evaluation design is flawed.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: The process of making a trained model available for real users, applications, or batch jobs to generate predictions or outputs.
cards.learningType: Engineering stage applicable to any trained model.
cards.taskType: Supports classification, regression, recommendation, forecasting, generation, and anomaly detection.
cards.highLevel: A model artifact is packaged with preprocessing and dependencies, then exposed through an API, batch scoring job, streaming service, edge device, or embedded application. Deployment includes versioning, rollback, logging, and security.
cards.whenUse: Use it when a model has passed evaluation and needs to deliver business value, such as scoring leads nightly, detecting fraud in real time, or serving recommendations on a website.
cards.limitations: Deployment can fail because of latency, dependency conflicts, data schema changes, scaling limits, security issues, or mismatch between training and live data. A good offline model is not automatically a good production system.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: Application Programming Interfaces are standardized ways for software systems to send data to a model service and receive predictions or generated outputs.
cards.learningType: Infrastructure/interface concept, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Supports online inference for classification, regression, search, recommendation, generation, and anomaly detection.
cards.highLevel: A client sends a request containing input features or text to an endpoint. The service validates the request, applies preprocessing, runs the model, postprocesses outputs, and returns a response in a defined format.
cards.whenUse: Use APIs when applications need real-time or near-real-time model outputs, such as fraud scoring during checkout, chatbot responses, or product recommendations.
cards.limitations: APIs introduce latency, rate limits, authentication requirements, versioning challenges, and failure modes. Poor schema design can cause client/server mismatch and hard-to-debug prediction errors.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: Ongoing measurement of model, data, and system behavior after deployment to detect performance degradation, latency problems, errors, bias, or unexpected usage patterns.
cards.learningType: Engineering/operations practice, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Supports all deployed ML systems.
cards.highLevel: Monitoring tracks input distributions, missing values, prediction distributions, latency, throughput, errors, business KPIs, and labeled performance when outcomes arrive. Alerts trigger investigation.
cards.whenUse: Use it for any production model, especially high-impact systems such as fraud, credit, medical triage, recommendations, or LLM assistants interacting with users.
cards.limitations: True labels often arrive late or never, so performance monitoring may rely on proxies. Too many alerts create fatigue, while too few miss silent failures.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: Techniques for identifying when live data, target relationships, or user behavior changes compared with training data, potentially reducing model reliability.
cards.learningType: Monitoring concept, not a model type, though it may use statistical or ML methods.
cards.taskType: Supports classification, regression, forecasting, recommendation, and generative systems.
cards.highLevel: It compares distributions of features, predictions, embeddings, labels, or residuals over time. Statistical tests, distance metrics, population stability index, and performance trends can indicate drift.
cards.whenUse: Use it after deployment when markets, customer behavior, sensors, policies, or product interfaces change. For example, a fraud model may drift after attackers change tactics.
cards.limitations: Not all drift hurts performance, and some performance drops occur without obvious feature drift. Thresholds are hard to set, and delayed labels make concept drift difficult to confirm.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: Updating a model by training it again on newer, corrected, expanded, or more representative data to restore or improve performance.
cards.learningType: Training/operations process applicable across learning paradigms.
cards.taskType: Supports classification, regression, forecasting, recommendation, anomaly detection, and LLM/domain adaptation workflows.
cards.highLevel: A retraining workflow collects fresh data, validates quality, rebuilds features, trains candidate models, evaluates against baselines, and deploys only if performance and safety checks pass.
cards.whenUse: Use it when monitoring shows drift, new labels accumulate, product behavior changes, or the model must learn new categories, seasons, fraud patterns, or business rules.
cards.limitations: Automatic retraining can propagate bad data or feedback loops if not governed. Retraining requires versioning, rollback plans, evaluation gates, and checks for leakage and fairness regression.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: A containerization tool that packages code, dependencies, runtime, and configuration into portable containers so ML services run consistently across environments.
cards.learningType: Infrastructure tool, not a learning paradigm.
cards.taskType: Supports deployment and reproducibility for all ML task types.
cards.highLevel: A Docker image defines the operating-system layer, packages, model files, application code, and startup command. Containers created from that image run similarly on laptops, servers, and cloud platforms.
cards.whenUse: Use it to deploy model APIs, batch jobs, training environments, reproducible experiments, or services with specific Python/CUDA/library versions.
cards.limitations: Containers do not solve bad code, data issues, or model quality. Images can become large, insecure, or hard to maintain, and GPU/CUDA compatibility still requires careful setup.

cards.heading: I. Practical ML engineering
cards.what: Core cloud concepts for ML, including compute instances, GPUs, object storage, managed databases, orchestration, permissions, networking, logging, and managed ML services.
cards.learningType: Infrastructure knowledge, not supervised or unsupervised.
cards.taskType: Supports training, deployment, monitoring, data processing, and storage for every task type.
cards.highLevel: ML workloads use cloud storage for datasets/artifacts, compute for training/inference, orchestration for scheduled jobs, and monitoring/logging for operations. Permissions control who and what can access resources.
cards.whenUse: Use cloud platforms when local machines are insufficient, when teams need shared infrastructure, scalable inference, GPUs, managed pipelines, or reliable production hosting.
cards.limitations: Cloud can be expensive and complex. Misconfigured permissions, uncontrolled GPU jobs, poor networking, or weak cost monitoring can create security and budget problems.

cards.heading: J. Applied areas
cards.what: The application area focused on enabling machines to analyze, understand, or generate visual data such as images, video, scans, and diagrams.
cards.learningType: Can be supervised, self-supervised, unsupervised, or generative depending on the task and labels.
cards.taskType: Classification, object detection, segmentation, regression, anomaly detection, tracking, retrieval, and generation.
cards.highLevel: Vision systems typically preprocess images, learn visual features using CNNs or vision transformers, and output labels, boxes, masks, embeddings, captions, or generated pixels.
cards.whenUse: Use it for medical-image analysis, manufacturing defect detection, autonomous systems, satellite imagery, OCR, face/object recognition, visual search, and content moderation.
cards.limitations: It needs representative visual data and careful labeling. Models can fail under lighting, camera, angle, demographic, or domain shifts, and privacy/ethics concerns are significant.

cards.heading: J. Applied areas
cards.what: Natural Language Processing is the application area concerned with analyzing, understanding, retrieving, translating, summarizing, or generating human language.
cards.learningType: Can be supervised, self-supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement/preference-tuned.
cards.taskType: Text classification, sequence labeling, semantic search, clustering, summarization, translation, question answering, generation, and extraction.
cards.highLevel: NLP systems tokenize text, convert it into embeddings, process it with models such as transformers, and produce labels, spans, rankings, summaries, translations, or generated responses.
cards.whenUse: Use it for support-ticket routing, document search, sentiment analysis, contract analysis, chatbots, knowledge-base assistants, summarization, and information extraction.
cards.limitations: Language is ambiguous, context-dependent, multilingual, and socially sensitive. Models can hallucinate, misunderstand nuance, encode bias, or fail on domain-specific terminology.

cards.heading: J. Applied areas
cards.what: Systems that predict and rank items a user may prefer, such as products, videos, songs, articles, jobs, or people.
cards.learningType: Often supervised or self-supervised from interaction data; can include reinforcement learning for long-term optimization.
cards.taskType: Ranking, classification, regression, retrieval, clustering, and personalization.
cards.highLevel: They combine user behavior, item features, context, and similarity signals. Common methods include collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, embeddings, two-tower retrieval, gradient-boosted ranking, and deep ranking models.
cards.whenUse: Use them when users face many choices and personalization can improve discovery, conversion, retention, or satisfaction, such as e-commerce, streaming, news, and learning platforms.
cards.limitations: They suffer from cold-start problems, feedback loops, popularity bias, filter bubbles, delayed feedback, and evaluation challenges because offline metrics may not match user satisfaction.

cards.heading: J. Applied areas
cards.what: Predicting future values ordered over time, such as demand, revenue, temperature, traffic, inventory, or sensor readings.
cards.learningType: Usually supervised because historical future values become labels; can include statistical, ML, and deep learning methods.
cards.taskType: Regression/forecasting; sometimes classification for event prediction or anomaly detection.
cards.highLevel: Models use past values, lag features, rolling statistics, seasonality, trends, holidays, and external variables to predict future time points. Evaluation must respect chronological order.
cards.whenUse: Use it for inventory planning, staffing, finance, energy load, website traffic, supply-chain planning, and capacity management.
cards.limitations: Forecasts fail when future conditions differ from history, events are unprecedented, or leakage occurs through random splits. Uncertainty intervals and business constraints are often as important as point forecasts.

cards.heading: J. Applied areas
cards.what: Applied detection of unusual behavior or observations in real-world systems, such as fraud, equipment failure, cyber intrusion, or abnormal medical readings.
cards.learningType: Often unsupervised or semi-supervised; supervised if labeled anomalies are available.
cards.taskType: Anomaly detection, rare-event classification, monitoring, and alerting.
cards.highLevel: Systems model normal patterns using rules, statistics, ML scores, reconstruction error, density, isolation, or forecasting residuals, then alert when observations exceed a threshold.
cards.whenUse: Use it in fraud monitoring, predictive maintenance, security operations, quality control, payment systems, and data observability.
cards.limitations: Rare events are hard to label and evaluate. High false-positive rates can overwhelm teams, while adaptive adversaries or changing systems can make old anomaly definitions obsolete.

cards.heading: J. Applied areas
cards.what: The application area where models create new content such as text, code, images, audio, video, molecules, designs, or synthetic data.
cards.learningType: Usually self-supervised pretraining with supervised fine-tuning, preference tuning, or reinforcement learning for alignment; some systems are conditional or multimodal.
cards.taskType: Generation, editing, summarization, transformation, question answering, code synthesis, and creative assistance rather than only classification/regression.
cards.highLevel: Generative models learn probability distributions or denoising processes from large datasets, then sample or decode new outputs conditioned on prompts, examples, images, audio, or other inputs.
cards.whenUse: Use it for drafting, coding help, design ideation, customer support, document summarization, image creation, data augmentation, tutoring, and workflow automation.
cards.limitations: Outputs can be wrong, biased, copyrighted, unsafe, or inconsistent with instructions. Production use requires evaluation, human oversight, privacy controls, security against prompt injection, and clear user expectations.
